units.text: Two observers find a perfect square in a particle distribution. The first says ‘the simulation grid’; the second, ‘the structure of space’. The observation is the same. What must be separated is not two exclamations, but models with different predictions.

This is the central difficulty. ‘We are in a simulation’ designates an enormous family of possibilities, not a unique mechanism. A simulation may approximate some processes or reproduce them exactly at the level accessible to observers. It may have a regular lattice, an adaptive representation or an implementation unlike a video game. That we use particular architectures does not oblige every possible simulator to use them.

Let us accept the generous condition that the simulator does not actively try to hide the implementation. Even then detection is not guaranteed. Lack of camouflage does not automatically produce an information leak. Two different mechanisms can have the same observable consequences, just as two programs can compute exactly the same function. If every accessible experiment has the same outcome distributions in the two models, no statistical ingenuity can create an absent difference. This is an identification limit, not a limit of the researcher’s courage.

An example of a more precise hypothesis was explored by Beane, Davoudi and Savage. They analyzed consequences of implementation on a cubic spacetime lattice under a particular Wilson-type discretization scheme. Such a construction can privilege certain directions and affect very energetic particles. The paper discusses constraints and possible signatures of that model; it offers no universal test for every simulated universe (Beane, Davoudi și Savage, 2014) .

The distinction is decisive. If we found anisotropy, a difference between directions, we would have a physical structure to explain. It could come from the proposed implementation model, a nonsimulated fundamental structure, particle sources, propagation or instruments. A positive result would not arrive labeled ‘external author’. A negative result would constrain certain implementations, not exclude every imaginable simulation.

Nor are quantum phenomena, by themselves, evidence that the world is computed only when we look. In physics, measurement involves physical interactions, not necessarily a human mind. Decoherence describes the loss of local access to interference through a system’s interaction with the environment and explains important aspects of classical behavior’s emergence. It does not alone resolve every dispute over quantum mechanics’ interpretation. But neither does it require a conscious spectator activating reality’s ‘rendering’ (Zurek, 2003) .

Indeed, a test attempting to discover whether the world computes details only on demand faces a problem: the very device intended to record the detail becomes a relevant interaction. We must specify what ‘on demand’ means in the simulation model and what different outcome distribution it produces. The analogy with saving resources in a game is not yet a physical prediction.

We could seek rounding errors, generator periodicity or resolution limits. But every proposal requires a sufficiently precise architecture. A finite sequence cannot alone prove that its source is fundamentally random; it can be reproduced by a program containing it. Conversely, unexpected regularity in a sequence does not prove a programmer’s existence. It may indicate an ununderstood physical process, data selection or an instrument defect.

More promising, at least logically, would be an anomaly that not only surprises but anticipates. An implementation model could predict a family of correlated deviations in advance: a particular energy dependence, orientation and ratio between quantities. If these relationships appeared in independent data, the model would gain support. It would still need comparison with physical explanations producing the same family of effects.

There is also the message scenario. Suppose a repeatable signal appears that responds to new challenges through controlled physical channels. After ordinary explanations were excluded, it would be an extraordinary discovery of a source capable of intelligent interaction. But ‘an intelligence communicates’ and ‘this intelligence is outside our universe’ are different conclusions. External origin must be supported separately, not extracted from spectacular content.

A project can be valuable without finding a simulation: it improves clocks, characterizes noise or tests symmetries. A weak project changes its explanation after every result and leaves nothing verifiable. Research productivity matters, not the amazement produced.
Some implementations might leave traces; others would remain undetectable. Research begins when the proposed mechanism precisely indicates what we should observe differently.
